Article Title: 'Better late than never': Why did F1 leave India, and why is it back on the agenda?
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Sebastian Vettel won the 2013 Indian Grand Prix, completing a hat-trick of victories at the Buddh International Circuit. It was also the day he sealed his fourth Formula 1 world championship. However, it turned out to be India's last Formula 1 race.The Indian Grand Prix ran for three years, from 2011 to 2013, but the race was suspended in 2014 and later disappeared from the calendar amid a tax dispute.Thirteen years later, the government has put Formula 1 back on its agenda.The Sports Ministry has formed a task force led by NITI Aayog's Yugal Kishore Joshi to work on the revival and development of Formula 1 and motorsports in India. The task force will assess the motorsports ecosystem, review the challenges that affected the sport in the past, and examine the feasibility of hosting a Formula 1 race, with a target of a possible return by 2028.But before India can look at a new Grand Prix, there is a question from the previous one that still needs answering: why did F1 leave India after just three races?The Buddh International Circuit was built in 2011 and was designed by German engineer Hermann Tilke.The dispute centred on the taxation of Formula 1 and its commercial activities in India. A key question was whether F1 should be classified as a sport or an entertainment business under Indian tax laws. The issue affected tax exemptions, customs duties and payments between race promoter and Formula 1's commercial rights holder.In 2017, the Supreme Court ruled that Formula 1's commercial rights company had a permanent establishment in India, making income linked to its Indian operations taxable.The ruling complicated the tax position and the financial obligations surrounding the Indian Grand Prix. Liberty Media, which acquired Formula 1's commercial rights in 2017, reportedly set aside USD 14.8 million to settle the tax liability.The problems, therefore, went beyond the cost of staging a race. The tax treatment of Formula 1, the movement of equipment across borders and the commercial structure surrounding the event had become major obstacles.The episode exposed a fundamental challenge for India: hosting a global sporting event requires more than a world-class venue. The regulatory framework, taxation rules and contractual arrangements must also work for an event that operates across international borders.The Sports Ministry's task force is now being asked to examine those problems and assess whether the conditions are different enough for India to try again."Basically, the task force will look into the possibilities and advise on how to move forward. It will assess the current situation, learn from the past, and identify the best way to take things forward, particularly in terms of development," FMSCI president Arindam Ghosh told TimesofIndia.com.The exercise could help establish what needs to change in the way India approaches international motorsport, from policy and taxation to operational clearances and the development of the wider racing ecosystem.Ghosh pointed to the growth of motorsport and the government's interest in developing the sport in India."Better late than never. Motorsport is gaining significant global popularity and is becoming increasingly prominent across the world. With the sport also expanding into more Asian countries, this is the right time for India to explore its return. The government recognises the growing importance of motorsport, so why not look at bringing it back?" he said.The audience for Formula 1 in India has also changed considerably since the last race.Formula 1 and FanCode state that the Indian fanbase had reached 79 million by late 2025. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali said in June 2026 that the figure had risen to 98 million, with 20 million fans added in the previous year.India has not hosted a Grand Prix since 2013, but its F1 audience has continued to grow.That presents a different opportunity from the one India had when it first hosted the championship. A return could connect an established global sporting property with a much larger domestic audience, including younger fans who have followed the sport through digital platforms and streaming.But a larger audience does not automatically translate into a viable race. India would still need to establish a sustainable arrangement with Formula 1, secure the necessary financial backing and ensure that the costs and regulatory obligations of hosting the event are manageable.The government can address policy and taxation, but Formula 1's return would also depend on a promoter willing to undertake the financial and organisational responsibility of staging a Grand Prix.The Indian Grand Prix was organised by the original developers of the Buddh International Circuit, which hosted Formula 1 races in Greater Noida from 2011 to 2013.The ownership landscape has since changed. The circuit's original parent group underwent insolvency proceedings, culminating in a ?14,535-crore acquisition of its flagship company by a new owner.The change could bring a different set of possibilities for the circuit, although any F1 revival would depend on a viable commercial arrangement and the necessary regulatory clearances.That change raises questions about the future arrangements for the circuit and the organisation of a possible Grand Prix. However, ownership of the venue is only one part of the equation. A race would also require agreement with Formula 1's commercial rights holder, a viable funding model, sponsors and broadcasting arrangements.Ghosh does not see sponsorship as the biggest obstacle."Not necessarily. The main reason was that no one took the initiative to bring Formula 1 back to India. Our economic conditions have improved significantly, so I don't think sponsorship will be a major problem," he said."Bringing F1 back would give a boost to the Indian economy, create opportunities in tourism and enhance the country's global standing. The World Rally Championship (WRC) is also in the pipeline. Both events have a strong fan following, and hosting them would be a matter of prestige for India, while also delivering economic and tourism benefits," Ghosh added.The challenge will be to translate that potential into a workable long-term plan. A Grand Prix requires substantial investment, and its viability depends on more than ticket sales or audience numbers. The arrangements must account for hosting fees, infrastructure, logistics, promotion and the wider economic benefits a race could generate.For India, the task force's assessment will be important in determining how those competing considerations can be balanced.Import duties were another issue during the earlier Indian Grand Prix, particularly for teams bringing equipment into the country. Formula 1 teams travel with specialised machinery, tools and technical equipment, much of which must cross international borders under strict schedules.Ghosh said the government is now looking at a system that could address that problem."Yes, import duties were one of the main reasons earlier, but I don't think they will be an issue anymore. The ministry is now clear about moving forward and has appointed a task force to look into these matters, including duty-related issues and a single-window clearance system to make it easier for teams and equipment to enter and leave the country," he said.A streamlined clearance process could reduce delays and simplify the movement of equipment. For a championship that operates to a tightly packed international calendar, predictable customs procedures and clear rules would be essential."The circuit is already there. The FIA's role will be to assess the technical requirements. It will inspect the track, after which the necessary upgrades will have to be carried out," Ghosh added.The existing infrastructure could give India a starting point, although a return would still require an assessment of the circuit by the FIA, the sport's governing body, as well as an agreement with Formula 1's commercial rights holder.The track's availability alone, therefore, cannot guarantee a place on the calendar. Technical compliance, operational readiness and a viable commercial agreement would all have to come together.That is where the task force's broader assessment becomes important.Akbar Ebrahim, a former Indian racer in Formula 2 and a three-term president of the Federation of Motor Sports Clubs of India, welcomed the government's decision to set up the task force."The federation did not set up the task force. It is being formed now by the government, through the Ministry of Sports and the honourable sports minister. This is a very positive development. It is encouraging to see the government taking an interest in motorsport, particularly Formula 1. In the past, motorsport did not receive the kind of attention it is getting today," Akbar told Timesofindia.com.He said the previous Indian Grand Prix should form an important part of the assessment."The task force can examine what went wrong previously, why the contract was not renewed and why the race was held in India for only three years. It can also assess what needs to be done now and whether bringing Formula 1 back is feasible," he added.For Ebrahim, that assessment cannot stop at the circuit."Formula 1 is a vast subject, and it is important for everyone involved to understand its entire ecosystem. This includes the circuit, organisational capabilities, requirements and commercial arrangements with Formula 1's commercial rights holder, the Liberty Group, as well as the FIA, the sport's world governing body, which oversees its technical and official aspects. The government needs to understand all these elements before making an informed decision on how to proceed. Setting up the task force is therefore a very good step," he said.His point is central to the revival debate. A Grand Prix is not simply a race weekend at an existing circuit. It involves coordination between the government, the venue, the championship's commercial rights holder, the governing body, the promoter and the various agencies responsible for delivering the event.India's previous experience offers a case study in what can go wrong when the arrangements surrounding an international sporting event become difficult to sustain.The prospect of a return has already brought back memories of the 2011-13 races. For younger fans who discovered Formula 1 through streaming, social media and Drive to Survive, a race at Buddh would be their first opportunity to watch the championship compete on home soil.There is excitement, but also scepticism over whether 2028 is realistic, given the crowded F1 calendar. Some fans are also asking for a longer-term commitment rather than another three-race association.For the government, the task force will now examine the issues that would have to be settled before a return.Its responsibilities include reviewing taxation and other policy barriers, evaluating infrastructure and operational requirements, assessing the economic, tourism, investment and international benefits of hosting major motorsport events, and preparing a roadmap for the development of motorsport.A policy framework, including possible public-private partnership models, is also expected to be considered.That work could determine whether India can create the conditions necessary to host Formula 1 on a sustainable basis, rather than treating a return as a one-off sporting spectacle.India has the Buddh International Circuit and a much larger F1 audience than it had when Vettel won the last Indian Grand Prix in 2013.The question now is whether the government can put the commercial and regulatory framework in place for Formula 1 to return - and stay.
Article Summary: The Indian Grand Prix ran for three years, from 2011 to 2013, but the race was suspended in 2014 and later disappeared from the calendar amid a tax dispute. The Sports Ministry has formed a task force led by NITI Aayog's Yugal Kishore Joshi to work on the revival and development of Formula 1. The task force will assess the motorsports ecosystem, review the challenges that affected the sport in the past, and examine the feasibility of hosting a race.

Article Title: 17-0! Indian rugby girls steal the show against New Zealand side
Article Text:
Image credit: Rugby India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

KOLKATA: Even as the Abhishek Sharma blitzkrieg dominated headlines in the morning, there was a different India-New Zealand sporting chatter that dominated social media in the evening.It was the video of one of the two successful tries by the Indian U20 women’s rugby sevens team against a team from heavyweights New Zealand comprising U20 Maori players from the country at Rajgir International Sports Complex on Tuesday.The match was a part of the India-New Zealand U20 Rugby Series as part of the 100 Years of Unity through Sport initiative.And while the Indian girls’ spectacular performance was against an invitational team from New Zealand, a 17-0 shut-out win over any All Blacks team deserves the attention the historic victory got around the country.The Indian squad put on a masterclass in structural discipline and tackle precision, storming to a 12–0 half-time lead before sealing the huge shutout with a final late try.“It was a once in a lifetime experience! I had only watched videos of the New Zealand teams’ matches before. It was great to be able to play with them,” India U20 player Akshaya NS said after the match as she shared a hug with her counterpart from New Zealand, Anyis Drossaerts Lake.While the team’s feat grabbed eyeballs on Tuesday, it was not the first achievement of an Indian women’s rugby team with the senior women’s national team attaining their best-ever Asian Games finish of sixth in Nagoya earlier this month. The Asiad campaign this time, that saw a lot of improvement from their show in Hangzhou 2022, was also the first time that an Indian women’s team had won two of its group games.There has been a steady development in Indian rugby since former South Africa rugby player moved to India in 2022, initially to work with Bihar Rugby, and has now been a member of the coaching staff and high-performance coach and scout for Rugby India.The U20 Rugby series under the 100 years’ initiative featured joint training sessions, cultural interactions and four Rugby Sevens matches, including, for the first time, two mixed-team matches in which players from India and New Zealand played together.“The mixed match was really fun as we got to play together after playing against one another,” Akshaya said pointing to Lake.“But one of the best experiences was watching a live Haka here in Rajgir in front of our very eyes,” added the excited Indian youngster.The New Zealand U20 Maori men’s team, before beating the Indian U20 men 32-0, gave everyone a taste of their culture with a Haka performance before the kick-off.The series emphasised the role of sport in advancing bilateral ties, cultural understanding and youth development, reflecting sport’s increasing importance in India’s international engagement and fostering a more connected global sporting community.It also built on an ongoing cooperation between Rugby India and New Zealand Rugby and in May this year, New Zealand Rugby coaching educators conducted a development programme for 35 Indian coaches at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar, aiming to enhance coaching capabilities and support rugby’s growth in India.As Rugby India chairman Rahul Bose put it, “The India-New Zealand U20 Rugby Series is about much more than the game itself. As we mark 100 years of sporting ties between our countries, bringing these young players together reflects the values that make rugby special: respect, teamwork and friendship.”Pic credit: Rugby India
Article Summary: The Indian U20 women’s rugby sevens team beat a team from New Zealand 17-0. The match was a part of the India-New Zealand U20 Rugby Series. The series is part of Rugby India's 100 Years of Unity through Sport initiative.

Article Title: Prakash Bhatt becomes second Indian after Javagal Srinath to be Test match referee
Article Text:
Prakash Bhatt during the toss between Bangladesh and West Indies (Image credit: BCB)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

MUMBAI: Former Saurashtra cricketer Prakash Bhatt on Wednesday made his ‘Test debut’ in Mirpur, Dhaka, in the first Test between Bangladesh and West Indies as a ICC match referee.Bhatt has thus become only the second Indian after ex-India pacer Javagal Srinath to become a match referee in Tests.In April this year, Bhatt had been chosen by the International Cricket Council in a newly created three-member Emerging panel of ICC international match referees.The ICC has an 'Elite panel' which has five match referees (Javagal Srinath, Andy Pycroft, Richie Richardson, Ranjan Madugalle and Jeff Crowe), with three referees from the newly created Emerging panel added to the list.The development meant that the ICC would post Bhatt to officiate in plenty of international games, including Test matches.Bhatt has been a BCCI match referee in domestic cricket since the 2007-2008 season. He has been an IPL match referee since 2018. He has been with the ICC since 2024. He is the first Indian to be included in the inaugural ICC Emerging panel of Match Referees.In his international career so far, Bhatt has officiated in 48 T20Is, six ODIs, four Women’s T20Is and three Women’s ODIs. He has also officiated in 67 first-class matches and 75 IPL matches so far. The 56-year-old Bhatt officiated in 13 matches in the Under-19 ODI World Cup held in Jan-Feb in Zimbabwe and Namibia. In Oct last year, Bhatt officiated in the Australia versus New Zealand T20I series in New Zealand.Bhatt played 51 first-class matches (3,183 runs at 39.29, seven centuries) and 38 List A matches (1,007 runs at 33.56, six fifties) between 1994-95 and 2004-05.
Article Summary: Prakash Bhatt made his 'Test debut' in the first Test between Bangladesh and West Indies. Bhatt has become only the second Indian after Javagal Srinath to become a match referee in Tests. The 56-year-old Bhatt officiated in 13 matches in the Under-19 ODI World Cup held in Jan-Feb in Zimbabwe and Namibia.

Article Title: ‘Stan the Man’ bows out: Wawrinka's illustrious tennis career ends in Basel
Article Text:
Switzerland's Stan Wawrinka (AP)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Stan Wawrinka’s professional tennis career came to a close on Tuesday after the three-time Grand Slam champion suffered a first-round defeat at the Swiss Indoors in Basel, his home tournament.The 41-year-old Swiss went down 7-5, 7-6 (2) to eighth seed Jiri Lehecka. His final shot as a professional was a backhand that sailed wide, drawing an audible reaction from the home crowd.Wawrinka, who turned professional in 2002, had announced last December that 2026 would be his final season on the tour. The veteran, popularly known as ‘Stan the Man’, received warm farewells at tournaments throughout his farewell year.Ahead of his last match, Wawrinka told the ATP Tour website that his career had always been guided by the desire to give his best and leave nothing unfinished.“For me, all I wanted in my career was to give everything, to have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100% in every match — out of respect for myself, for the opponent, for the tournament, for the fans, for everybody," he said.“That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and that's the only way you can leave the sport: without any regrets.”Wawrinka’s career was defined by three memorable Grand Slam triumphs, each secured against a player who was ranked world No. 1 at the time of the final.He defeated Rafael Nadal to lift the Australian Open title in 2014 before beating Novak Djokovic in the 2015 French Open final. He overcame Djokovic again in the 2016 US Open final to claim his third major crown.The Swiss reached a career-best ranking of world No. 3 in 2014 and finished his career with 16 tour-level titles.His achievements also included success alongside compatriot Roger Federer . The pair won the doubles gold medal at the 2008 Beijing Olympics before helping Switzerland secure its first Davis Cup title in 2014.Wawrinka’s exit in Basel brought the curtain down on a career that spanned more than two decades and included some of the biggest victories of his generation.
Article Summary: Stan Wawrinka's professional tennis career came to a close on Tuesday. The 41-year-old Swiss went down 7-5, 7-6 (2) to eighth seed Jiri Lehecka. He announced last December that 2026 would be his final season on the tour.

Article Title: Cricket Australia Revenue: India series drive record Cricket Australia revenue, two-day Ashes Tests burn A$20m hole in finances
Article Text:
Rohit Sharma, left, and Virat Kohli return to the pavilion after winning the third ODI match of a series against Australia, at the Sydney Cricket Ground, in Sydney, Australia. (PTI File Photo)

Two-day Ashes Tests cost CA A$20 million

Cricket Australia's (CA) record revenue of A$601.1 million ($423 million) in the 2025-26 financial year was driven by media rights deals for the Ashes and the limited-overs series against India. The governing body also reported a net surplus of A$81.8 million ($57 million), but two Ashes Tests that ended inside two days last summer cost it an estimated A$20 million in revenue.The financial impact comes as CA prepares for two consecutive years of projected losses, with deficits expected in 2026-27 and 2027-28.On Wednesday, Cricket Australia said its financial results for 2025-26 reflected strong commercial performance, record audiences and the success of the international season. In the previous financial year, 2024-25, it had recorded a net loss of A$11.3 million ($7.95 million).CA said the men's home Ashes series against England and the white-ball series against India generated record media, commercial and match-day revenue. However, it expects revenue to fall over the next two financial years due to a “cyclical decline in media rights and match revenues in line with the international touring schedule.”The financial outlook does not include the anticipated sale of stakes in some Big Bash League (BBL) franchises.Australia's teams also enjoyed success on the field during the year. The men's side retained the Ashes with a 4-1 series win at home, while the women's team won its seventh ICC T20 World Cup title after beating England in the final at Lord's.During October and November last year, Australia won the ODI series against India 2-1, while India claimed the T20I series by the same margin.The Ashes also drew record crowds, with 859,580 spectators attending matches over 18 days, at an average of 47,754 per day.Despite the record financial results, the two Ashes Tests that ended inside two days dealt a significant blow to CA's revenue. The initial estimate for the loss from the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) Test was A$10 million, but the final impact was higher. The Perth Test, which also failed to reach a third day, added to the shortfall.At Wednesday's annual general meeting, outgoing CA chair Mike Baird joked about the need for future Test matches to last the full five days while addressing his successor, former Australia batter David Boon.“We’ve had a record Ashes crowd at the MCG, 94,000, only going two days there,” Baird said. “Let’s mark it down that five-day Tests are a good thing, Boonie.”The combined revenue hit from the two shortened Tests amounted to A$20 million, adding to the challenges facing CA as it prepares for two years of projected losses.
Article Summary: Cricket Australia's record revenue of A$601.1 million ($423 million) in the 2025-26 financial year was driven by media rights deals for the Ashes and the limited-overs series against India. Two Ashes Tests that ended inside two days last summer cost it an estimated A$20 million in revenue. Financial impact comes as CA prepares for two consecutive years of projected losses, with deficits expected in 2026-27 and 2027-28.

Article Title: Asian Champions Trophy Hockey: India look to continue winning run against China
Article Text:
Image credit: Hockey India

Mandeep makes a strong statement

Fulton wants India to improve after the break

China present a different challenge

India squad

India will look to build on their strong start to the Asian Champions Trophy when they face China in their second round-robin match on Thursday. The five-time champions began their title defence with a big win over Bangladesh and will be keen to maintain their momentum against a young Chinese side.India, who recently won their second successive Asian Games gold medal to secure direct qualification for the Los Angeles Olympics, dominated Bangladesh in their opening match. Bangladesh replaced Pakistan in the tournament after the latter refused to travel to India, citing security reasons.The match was largely played in Bangladesh's half, with India controlling the contest. While Bangladesh were not expected to pose a major challenge, India's ability to score from both field play and penalty corners was an encouraging sign.The Harmanpreet Singh-led side scored eight field goals and five goals from set pieces against Bangladesh on Tuesday.Veteran forward Mandeep Singh was among the standout performers, scoring a hat-trick. His return to form comes at an important time, with national selectors expected to assess the players after the tournament.Mandeep was reportedly among four senior players who could be phased out after the ACT.The other three were Jarmanpreet Singh, Amit Rohidas and Nilakanta Sharma.Nilakanta announced on Tuesday that the tournament would be his last at the international level. However, Mandeep and Jarmanpreet are keen to continue playing.Apart from Mandeep's three goals, captain Harmanpreet, Dilpreet Singh and vice-captain Hardik Singh scored twice each. Shilanand Lakra, Nilakanta and Jugraj Singh also got on the scoresheet.India chief coach Craig Fulton was pleased with Mandeep's performance."He (Mandeep) was good, he did full of running and was nice and sharp, which was important," he said.Despite the convincing result, Fulton felt India needed to perform better in the third quarter, after the teams changed ends."We wanted a fast start, which we got in the first quarter. We wanted to play some fast-flowing hockey, which we did. But the third quarter wasn't that good, and that remains a problem. But I am glad we finished strongly," he pointed out.India had to manage without midfielder Manpreet Singh, who has been ruled out of the tournament because of a calf muscle injury. Hardik, Vivek Sagar Prasad and Nilakanta took charge of the midfield against Bangladesh and combined well with the forwards.Mandeep was a major threat in attack, with Abhishek, Dilpreet, Shilanand and Sukhjeet Singh supporting him.At the back, Harmanpreet, Amit Rohidas, Jugraj and Sanjay will continue to shoulder responsibility, while Suraj Karkera and Krishan Bahadur Pathak are the goalkeeping options.India will face a less familiar opponent in China, who pushed Asian Games silver medallists Malaysia hard before going down 4-5 in their opening match.China have brought an entirely new squad for the tournament, with their young players showing promise against Malaysia. Their lack of recent exposure against India, however, makes them a difficult team to assess.Fulton admitted that India had limited information about their opponents."This Chinese team is unknown to us, as they have come here with a completely new group, not the one that played at the Asian Games. We don't know much about them and haven't seen them play. We will have to analyse video footage of their match to get a fair idea about them," Fulton said.India will aim to carry their attacking form into Thursday's match while addressing the concerns raised by their coach. China, meanwhile, will look to build on their close contest against Malaysia and challenge the defending champions.Malaysia will face South Korea, while Japan will take on Bangladesh in the other matches scheduled for Thursday.Goalkeepers: Suraj Karkera, Krishan Bahadur PathakDefenders: Sanjay, Harmanpreet Singh (captain), Amit Rohidas, Jugraj Singh, Jarmanpreet Singh, Amandeep LakraMidfielders: Rajinder Singh, Aditya Arjun Lalage, Nilakanta Sharma, Hardik Singh, Vivek Sagar PrasadForwards: Shilanand Lakra, Abhishek, Sukhjeet Singh, Dilpreet Singh, Mandeep Singh
Article Summary: India will face China in their second round-robin match on Thursday. The five- time champions began their title defence with a big win over Bangladesh. Harmanpreet Singh-led side scored eight field goals and five goals from set pieces against Bangladesh.

When some of India's best school-level basketball talent returned from the Rising Stars Invitational in Singapore earlier this year, Sunny Malik asked them what they had learnt from the tournament. Their answer was straightforward. They had struggled to keep pace as the game wore on, and their stamina and endurance needed work.“They said that the level of competition showed us that we need to improve a lot more. We ended up lacking in stamina and endurance. That’s what those kids told me,” Malik, NBA India Country Head, told TimesofIndia.com on the sidelines of ACG Jr. NBA 3v3 National Tournament in Delhi last week.“Imagine the kind of learning that they have through that one game stating that by third quarter we were lot of losing it and fourth quarter we were down.”The players were already looking ahead to the next edition. They told Malik they would work on those weaknesses before returning to Singapore.“They said that if we are the best team in India next year and we participate in RSI next year, we assure you that we will go to at least semis.Because we will work on our stamina, we will work on our endurance and we will work on the weaknesses that we saw through the entire program,” he said.“That is what we want kids to know.”Malik returned to that experience while discussing the ACG Jr. NBA 3v3 National Tournament, where teams from schools with established basketball programmes competed alongside those from schools without the same infrastructure.The 2026 edition has moved from the under-14 to the under-16 category. The 10-city competition began in September and will culminate in national finals in December.Delhi recorded 270 team registrations across 118 schools: 193 boys’ teams and 77 girls’ teams.For Malik, the tournament is an opportunity for players to discover the standard of competition beyond their own schools and assess what it takes to keep up.“The overall exposure and learning that they can get through this program, playing against the best teams coming in from a city or the outskirts of that city, is the main objective is,” he said.During a girls’ game in Delhi, the difference in positioning was evident. In the half-court format, with 12 seconds to attack, one team struggled to find its positions while the other exploited the gaps. Malik, responding to the observation, said the difference was down to strategy rather than size.“Somewhere these kids are playing better because they are not bigger than their opposition; they [opposition] are playing better because their strategy is better,” Malik said.He sees that contrast between schools that have a structured basketball programme and those where children learn largely through experience. “And that's where I see the difference between a school having a basketball program and school not having a basketball program because, you know, then they are running ad hoc, wanting to work not through a strategy but through their individual learning,” he said.“Whereas a school having a basketball program teaches you about this positioning, how do you pass, how do you ensure that you are able to score a bucket in that time that you have got.”The technical side of the game is only one part of what young players need to develop. Malik said the Singapore experience had also brought the physical and mental demands of international competition into focus.“Personally, when I saw a lot of these teams playing at RSI, I felt the one thing that a lot of our teams have to work on is endurance, stamina building, mental conditioning,” he said.“Playing against the best in the world requires that toughness, that endurance, that you will continue for those four quarters at your peak.”The Singapore experience also sharpened Malik’s view of what needs attention away from competition. He believes coaching development is one area of Indian sport that still requires more investment.“Coaches development is one area which probably, and that's my personal take, gets ignored sometimes,” he said. “But that's a very, very important part of the overall ecosystem development.”“Unless you invest in coaches, unless you support coaches with a training level which is world class, how do those coaches produce world-class talent? So investment in coaching, infra coaching ecosystem is an important part that every organisation should look into which is invested in sports. Only then can you produce world-class athletes from that.”The Jr. NBA programme has been running in India since 2013, reaching more than 15 million young people and 15,000 physical education instructors across 35 cities.International coaches, including Natalia André, have been involved in coaching clinics and development work across the region. But Malik acknowledged the limits of a programme that moves between cities over a few days.“That's challenging. If it's a five-day program in the city, the best that you can do is train some of the coaches,” he said.“The best that you can do is, if you genuinely see some talent, you can sit with them, spend some time and explain them that where were they lacking so that they take those learning out of coaches like Natalia who is coming from outside world and seeing the best kids playing in the APAC or across the globe.”The work with coaches is intended to continue after the tournament teams leave. Malik said the programme had used coaching clinics to introduce local instructors to the curriculum and standards followed by international coaches.“Through the global coaches that we have, coaching clinics with them, trying to tell them what the right level of coaching is, what kind of curriculum do we follow,” he said.He put the responsibility on those coaches to keep children playing once the tournament window closes. “The objective is that participation should not stop once the program gets over,” Malik said.“So if it's a four-month program, you don't want kids to only play for four months. You want them to play through the year. And for that, these coaches have to play an important role in conditioning them, welding on the learnings that they have drawn through this competition, and then improving on those.”Malik said the coaching ecosystem had improved, but still needed support and investment if India was to produce world-class players.The Delhi numbers also reflect a broader feature of the Jr. NBA programme: girls’ participation. Malik said some city-level competitions had recorded girls’ participation of around 40-45%, a figure he found encouraging.“I personally don't see a lot of sports where girls participation is as high as 45% in a city-level competition,” he said.“So, girls participation at 40-45% encourages us a lot that through this program you are also bringing in girls into the mainstream of sports. And that's one of the big objectives that we have.”The tournament’s national finals are another step for teams that progress through the city competitions. After holding the finals in Delhi for the previous two years, organisers intend to stage this year’s event in Chennai.Malik said changing the venue would give players experience of competing in a different city and arena. “Because if these kids have to play at national level, they will be, you know, going across the country. You don't want to just stay to one location,” he said.“Similarly, ACG Junior NBA finals across different cities would always, you know, be helpful for these kids who are getting into a final. They are getting into more exposure into a different city, different environment, different arena, different exposure.”The top two boys’ teams and top two girls’ teams from each city, along with selected all-star teams, are set to qualify for the December finals.Whether the competition can help players move towards professional basketball is a separate question. A proposed Indian basketball league could provide another platform. For Malik, though, its talent-identification process would become clearer as the plans take shape.“I think anything which helps basketball in the country, NBA would always be the first one to support that initiative. We would love to support any initiative which gets kids the pathway that they are looking at,” he said.“Getting kids the pathway, getting kids the right platform to showcase their talent is a great initiative. We are definitely in support of anything which helps basketball in the country.”He also wants the sport to attract a wider audience. “As a category, it's important for basketball to become prime time. As a category, it's important for people to watch, people to play, people to participate. We are in support of any initiative helping basketball.”Asked whether players in the under-16 tournament could progress into the proposed league, Malik said he was not privy to its structure or the plans of its coaches and scouts.He did, however, point to the existing partnership between ACG and the Jr. NBA programme, saying players who performed well could come to the attention of organisations looking for talent.“Some of these talents, which would do well at these levels, would automatically form a part of the larger talent pool, which would be visible to everyone,” he said.The under-16 tournament offers a competitive platform, but what happens after December will depend in part on whether players continue to train and compete. Malik’s expectation is clear: the four-month programme should not be the only time they play.
Article Summary: ACG Jr. NBA 3v3 National Tournament took place in Delhi last week. 10-city competition began in September and will culminate in national finals in December. Delhi recorded 270 team registrations across 118 schools: 193 boys' teams and 77 girls' teams.

Article Title: EFI mess costs Indian riders global stage, FEI ban from Dec 1
Article Text:
Equestrian Federation of India

New Delhi:

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe the governance crisis at the Equestrian Federation of India will negatively impact athletes' futures? Yes, definitely No, it won't 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Yet another tale of administrative chaos and athletes paying the price. Caught in a prolonged governance crisis at the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI), Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes’ exposure to global competition.The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections, effectively shutting Indian riders, officials, trainers and horses out of international events. TOI is in possession of FEI’s Oct 15 letter confirming the decision, which was taken at the international body's board meeting on Oct 13.Explaining its move, the FEI said the EFI’s prolonged governance crisis had reached a tipping point. “The absence of elections to date to elect a new Executive Committee, has resulted in a prolonged governance and leadership irregularity that is no longer sustainable,” the letter by FEI Governance Director Francisco Lima stated.The crisis follows the Delhi high court’s dissolution of the EFI executive committee in Feb 2026. Its elected tenure had expired in Sept 2023, while fresh elections remain pending nine months after the court’s intervention. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) constituted an ad hoc committee on March 27 to oversee the federation and facilitate the electoral process.While acknowledging the committee’s Sept 27 submission and its work, the FEI said elections were expected by Jan 31, 2027. However, the suspension will be reviewed only after the polls are held and evaluated by the international body.The consequences are sweeping. Citing its statutes, the FEI said the EFI “may not attend or be represented at any session or meeting of any FEI body, nor may it organise international events.” More damagingly, athletes, officials, trainers and horses “may not participate in international events organised by the FEI or any other national federation, whether under the Indian flag or the FEI flag.”With the suspension taking effect before the stated election deadline, Indian riders risk losing crucial international competition opportunities. Their return will depend on the completion of elections and the FEI’s subsequent evaluation, leaving athletes caught in a governance crisis they did not create.
Article Summary: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections. Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes' exposure to global competition.

Article Title: SA vs AUS: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after helmet blow, returns to field in Durban Test
Article Text:
Steve Smith

Smith's concussion history raises concern after helmet blow

Australia close in on victory as South Africa lose two wickets

Former Australia captain Steve Smith has been cleared of concussion and resumed fielding duties on the fifth day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, after undergoing a series of clinical assessments following a blow to the helmet.The 37-year-old batter was struck by a short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje during Australia's second innings. Smith attempted to duck under the ball but misjudged its trajectory as it failed to rise as much as he expected.Although he continued batting after the incident, scoring 27 off 41 balls before being caught at long-on off Simon Harmer, Smith did not take the field when South Africa began their second innings on Monday. Michael Neser served as his substitute fielder during that session.However, Smith returned to the field on Tuesday morning after being cleared under Cricket Australia's concussion protocols. He was stationed in the slip cordon when South Africa resumed their chase and subsequently took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling."Steve Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning," Cricket Australia said in a statement.The incident brought back memories of Smith's previous concussion scare during the 2019 Ashes in England, when he was struck on the head by fast bowler Jofra Archer and forced to miss part of a Test match.Smith's return to the field came after medical assessments over the preceding 24 hours, with Australia following the prescribed protocols before allowing the experienced batter to resume his duties.His presence was a boost for Australia as they pushed for victory in the series opener, with South Africa mounting a determined resistance on the final day.South Africa resumed at 102/4 on Tuesday, needing another 319 runs to win. They reached 166/6 by lunch after Australia struck twice to strengthen their grip on the contest.Opener Aiden Markram led the home side's resistance, remaining unbeaten on 69 at the interval alongside Marco Jansen on seven. The pair had to rebuild after Wiaan Mulder's patient 69-run fifth-wicket partnership with Markram ended when Josh Hazlewood had Mulder caught behind by Alex Carey.Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw then dismissed Verreynne, who made just one before edging a reckless shot to Smith at slip.Renshaw has been Australia's standout performer with the bat, having scored 190 in the first innings and 82 in the second, before adding two wickets to his match contribution.Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test. The second Test of the series is scheduled to begin in Gqeberha on Sunday.
Article Summary: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after blow to the helmet. Former Australia captain was struck by short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje. Smith took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling. Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test.

The SA20 Season 5 auction will see 156 cricketers go under the hammer on October 7, with former Joburg Super Kings captain Faf du Plessis Rassie van der Dussen and all-rounder Wiaan Mulder among the leading South African names available.The shortlist was trimmed down from 789 players who initially registered for the auction. Article Title: 'Why not play him?': Ex-India cricketer calls for big change in 4th T20I vs New Zealand
Article Text:
BCCI Photo

Chopra wants Mayank to replace Arshdeep

‘If Ishan Kishan is available, he has to walk into the team’

Chopra questions calls to drop Shreyas or Tilak

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India have already taken an unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match T20I series against New Zealand. With the series decided, former India opener Aakash Chopra wants the team management to give another opportunity to Mayank Yadav in the fourth T20I.Chopra believes Mayank should replace Arshdeep Singh in the playing XI for the match in Auckland on Friday, October 30. He also wants Prince Yadav to retain his place in the team.Speaking in a video on his YouTube channel, ‘Aakash Chopra’, the former cricketer said India should use the remaining matches to give opportunities to young players.Chopra believes India can make one change to their playing XI for the fourth T20I. He wants Arshdeep to be rested and Mayank to return to the side."There is scope for one change for sure. Ask Arshdeep Singh to rest. Play both Mayank and Prince because you give chances to youngsters in dead rubbers. Mayank actually bowled well in the first match. So., why not play him? I am advocating for that one change," he said.Mayank played only the first T20I of the series, taking 1/40 in his four overs. Chopra believes the young fast bowler deserves another chance, especially with India having already won the series.The former opener also backed Bhuvneshwar Kumar to play all five matches, despite the senior pacer's struggles in the first three games."I won't talk about playing spin here because there is actually no help for spinners here. You have to bowl short balls and make the batters access the side boundaries. The spinners can't do that job. The fast bowlers can do that job. It might not be going well for Bhuvi, but he should be played all five games," he observed.Bhuvneshwar has taken one wicket in the first three T20Is and has an economy rate of 11.58. Chopra, however, feels the experienced seamer should continue to get opportunities.Chopra also discussed the possibility of Ishan Kishan returning to the playing XI if he is fit and available. However, he admitted that bringing the wicketkeeper-batter back into the side would create a selection challenge.The former India player suggested that the team might need to rotate its four top-order batters to accommodate everyone."If Ishan Kishan is available, he has to walk into the team. If he comes, who will go out? It is not an easy decision. You may be the best player on the planet, but since we have to accommodate Vaibhav Suryavanshi and we want to keep all four together, I think you will have to take the support of rotation," he said.Kishan's return would leave the team management with a difficult decision about who should make way. Chopra pointed out that dropping either Shreyas Iyer or Tilak Varma would not be an easy call.Some fans have suggested dropping Shreyas or Tilak to make room for the other top-order batters. Chopra disagreed with that approach, pointing to Tilak's contribution in India's recent win and asking why Shreyas should be dropped after just two poor matches."Someone said Shreyas should be dropped. Someone wrote below that Tilak should be dropped. I said, 'Don't you watch the match.' Tilak Varma won the match just now. How will you drop Tilak Varma? Shreyas Iyer had two bad matches, and you are saying he should be dropped," Chopra observed.Chopra admitted that he did not have a clear answer to the selection question. He said Shreyas and head coach Gautam Gambhir would have to make the final decision.The fourth T20I in Auckland will give India an opportunity to test their options before the final match of the series. With the trophy already secured, the team management could use the remaining games to assess its bench strength and manage the workload of its regular players.
Article Summary: Chopra believes India can make one change to their playing XI for the fourth T20I. He wants Arshdeep to be rested and Mayank to return to the side. Chopra also backs Bhuvneshwar Kumar to play all five matches.

Article Title: Steve Smith's neck injury forces extended layoff, Cricket Australia reveals return timeline
Article Text:
Australia's Steve Smith (AP)

Inglis makes an immediate impact

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Australian batter Steve Smith has been ruled out of selection until the home Test series against New Zealand in December after scans confirmed a cervical facet joint injury in his neck.Cricket Australia revealed the extent of Smith's injury after he was forced to withdraw from the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town, which began on Tuesday. The 37-year-old experienced neck pain on the fourth day of the second Test in Gqeberha last week and was subsequently ruled unfit for the series decider."Steve Smith developed neck pain on day four of the second Test in Gqeberha last week," Cricket Australia said in a statement."Subsequent MRI imaging confirmed a cervical facet joint injury. Due to this and his limited range of motion, he was unfit to participate in the current Test."Smith will continue with treatment and rehabilitation, with Australia expecting him to be available again for the New Zealand series at home in December."Steve will continue to receive treatment and rehabilitation, with a full return to availability anticipated for the upcoming home Test series against New Zealand," the statement added.In Smith's absence, Josh Inglis was brought into the side and made the most of his opportunity, scoring an unbeaten 85 as Australia reached 330/4 in reply to South Africa's first-innings total of 329.The hosts held a slender one-run lead at the close.Matt Renshaw contributed 74, while Cameron Green scored 65 and Alex Carey remained unbeaten on 51. Marnus Labuschagne, however, endured another disappointing outing, departing for a duck.South Africa had earlier been bowled out for 329 after Australia elected to field first. Aiden Markram scored 78, Marques Ackermann made 95 and Marco Jansen added 52 before Mitchell Starc claimed six wickets for 72 runs to wrap up the innings.The Cape Town Test marked Inglis' first appearance in the longest format since he played against England in Adelaide during the Ashes series at the end of last year.Renshaw praised his team-mate's response after Australia lost two quick wickets, saying Inglis' positive approach had helped the side regain momentum."He is a very talented player, we have seen that across a lot of the white-ball formats," Renshaw said."To come in today, we were under a little bit of pressure, having lost two quick wickets, and the way that he played was really positive – it was a very Josh innings, and I think it was really what we needed at that time," he added.
Article Summary: Steve Smith ruled out of third Test against South Africa with neck injury. Smith will continue with treatment and rehabilitation, with Australia expecting him to be available again for the New Zealand series at home in December. Josh Inglis makes most of his opportunity, scoring 85 as Australia reach 330/4 in reply to South Africa's first-innings total of 329.

Article Title: ‘I think about going for a boundary off the very first ball’: Tilak Varma on his new role for India
Article Text:
Tilak Varma (ANI Photo)

‘The bowler is under far more pressure’

India eye 5-0 series sweep

India vice-captain Tilak Varma says his move from No. 3 to the middle order has brought a shift in his batting approach, with the left-hander now looking to attack from the outset whenever the opportunity presents itself.Tilak, who has established himself as a reliable performer in run chases over the past 12 months, has adapted to batting at No. 5 or 6 by balancing his attacking instincts with the need to take the game deep."I already had the power game; I have scored runs at number three as well. Now, batting at number five or six, I think about going for a boundary off the very first ball only if it's there to be hit," he said ahead of the fourth T20I against New Zealand."Otherwise, I focus on taking the game deep. I take a bit more time. Initially, I focus on singles and doubles, finding gaps for fours or two runs," he added.The approach has served him well, including during India's tense chase in the second T20I against New Zealand, when he combined with Nitish Kumar Reddy to guide the team through a difficult situation. India have since taken an unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match series.Tilak believes managing the pressure on bowlers is an important part of his approach during the closing stages of a chase. Rather than allowing the situation to dictate his decisions, he tries to remind himself that the bowler is the one facing greater pressure."In the end overs, as a batsman, the bowler is under far more pressure than I am. That positive thought is constantly running in my head, that the bowler is under more pressure, so they are bound to leak runs."Recalling his crucial partnership with Reddy at Hagley Oval, Tilak said he encouraged his batting partner to remain at the crease and keep the chase alive rather than worry about the result."I just told Nitish, 'if we pull the match off from here, it's going to be immense fun. Let's just stay out there, take the game deep, and see what happens'."Despite having already clinched the series, India are not planning to ease off in the remaining matches. Tilak said the team wants to make the most of the opportunity to complete a clean sweep."We are thinking this is a great opportunity to achieve a clean sweep. The next goal is to win the upcoming match and give the Indian crowd a great chance to witness a 5–0 series win."The Indian team arrived in New Zealand shortly after completing its series against the West Indies at home. Tilak acknowledged that adapting to different conditions and a new time zone was challenging, but insisted that the players could not use it as an excuse."At this level, we cannot make excuses. We are at the highest level, and we need to set standards for the youngsters who look up to us."Gautam sir (head coach Gautam Gambhir) made it clear in team meetings that this is a long tour and the standard we set as a T20 side will provide momentum for the ODI and Test squads," added Tilak.With the T20I series already secured, India will look to maintain their momentum and carry the same standards into the remaining fixtures of the New Zealand tour.
Article Summary: India vice-captain Tilak Varma says his move from No. 3 to the middle order has brought a shift in his batting approach. The left-hander now looks to attack from the outset whenever the opportunity presents itself. Tilak believes managing the pressure on bowlers is an important part of his approach during the closing stages of a chase.

Article Title: After Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, meet Uma Kashvi: 15-year-old Karnataka all-rounder who became youngest player bought at WPL auction
Article Text:
Uma Kashvi (Image-X)

From a junior double century to age-group dominance

516 runs at an average of 172

Delhi Capitals see long-term potential

Delhi Capitals complete 17-member squad

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of Uma Kashvi's game excites you the most? Her batting skills Her bowling ability Her leadership experience Her achievements at a young age 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Indian cricket has found another teenage prospect to watch, with Karnataka's Uma Kashvi making history at the Women's Premier League (WPL) 2027 auction in Kochi on October 28.Delhi Capitals signed the 15-year-old for Rs 10 lakh, making her the youngest player ever to be bought at a WPL auction. At 15 years and 202 days, Kashvi surpassed the previous record held by Deeya Yadav, who was 16 when she was bought at last year's auction.While Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has attracted attention with his rise in men's cricket, Kashvi is beginning to make her mark in the women's game. A right-arm off-spinner who can contribute with the bat in the middle order, she has progressed through Karnataka's age-group system and represented India Under-19 against Sri Lanka in 2026.Her WPL debut, however, could be delayed as she is part of India's Under-19 World Cup plans. The tournament, scheduled to be held in Bangladesh and Nepal, overlaps with the WPL.Kashvi's cricketing journey began at around seven and a half years of age, when she started training at an academy near her home. Her potential soon became evident, with the youngster scoring an unbeaten 217 in a junior club-level inter-school tournament in Bengaluru at just 12.Her exposure to the wider cricketing world came even earlier. At nine, she received the Young Talent Award at the India Nippon Cup, where she shared a dressing room with India internationals Veda Krishnamurthy, Jemimah Rodrigues, Deepti Sharma and Shreyanka Patil.Kashvi has since taken on leadership responsibilities, captaining Karnataka's Under-15 team and leading Bengaluru Blasters in the Maharani Trophy, Karnataka's women's T20 competition. In the 2025 tournament, she scored 48 off 42 balls against Mysore Warriors, gaining experience against senior domestic players.She also featured in Karnataka's Under-19 T20 campaign and the side that reached the semi-finals of the Women's Under-19 One-Day Trophy.Her performances earned her an opportunity with India Under-19 against Sri Lanka in June and July 2026. Kashvi picked up four wickets in three T20 matches and two wickets in two one-day games.Kashvi's batting credentials received further confirmation during the Women's Under-15 One-Day Trophy in the 2025-26 season, where she finished as the leading run-scorer.She amassed 516 runs at an average of 172, registering three centuries and a half-century. One of her standout performances came against Manipur on January 10, 2026, when she smashed an unbeaten 158 off just 66 balls, hitting 23 fours and seven sixes.Her innings helped Karnataka post 321/5 in 35 overs at the Aditya Academy Ground in Kolkata. Karnataka went on to win the match by 275 runs.Kashvi has also shown her ability to influence games with the ball. In Karnataka's Under-19 T20 Trophy quarter-final against Vidarbha on October 22, 2026, she returned figures of 3/18 in four overs. She also scored 11 off 13 balls as Karnataka defended 140/7 to win by six runs. Her all-round contribution earned her the Player of the Match award.Delhi Capitals head coach Jonathan Batty said the franchise had been monitoring Kashvi for some time, with its scouting network playing a key role in the decision to sign her.“She has been on our radar for a little while. Our scouts have watched her play extensively and shared some incredible feedback, and I have seen her play as well. We believe she could become an absolute superstar in the future," said Batty.Batty also made it clear that the franchise views the teenager's signing as a long-term investment rather than an expectation of immediate results.“At 15, she is very much a work in progress, and we are not expecting her to be the finished article just yet. This is a long-term project for Delhi Capitals."He added that training alongside experienced players and working with the franchise's coaching staff could help accelerate her development.“It is a wonderful opportunity for her to be part of this setup, learn from our top coaches and work alongside international stars. Hopefully, she will learn a huge amount from the players around her. This is the first step on a journey that we hope will lead to Indian recognition in the future, and we’re excited to see her progress,” Batty continued.Delhi Capitals picked up four players at the Kochi auction, adding Kashvi, explosive Indian batter Kiran Navgire, Indian all-rounder Nazma Khan and Scotland spinner Kirstie Gordon to a core of 13 retained players.Navgire was their biggest acquisition at Rs 75 lakh, while Kashvi, Khan and Gordon were each bought for Rs 10 lakh. The franchise spent Rs 1.05 crore at the auction, taking its total squad expenditure to Rs 14.95 crore, including Rs 13.9 crore on retentions.For Kashvi, the move marks an important step in a journey that has already featured age-group records, domestic success and international junior cricket. Delhi Capitals will now provide her with an opportunity to learn from established players as she continues to develop her game.
Article Summary: Uma Kashvi is the youngest player ever to be bought at a Women's Premier League auction. Delhi Capitals signed the 15-year-old for Rs 10 lakh. Kashvi surpassed the previous record held by Deeya Yadav, who was 16.

Article Title: Perfect pairing? Why India must stick with Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
Article Text:
Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (BCCI Photo)

With the T20I series against New Zealand already sealed, the pressure on India to pick the safest XI might have eased. Maybe the team management can focus on a more important question: what should India’s batting order look like two years from now, when the 2028 T20 World Cup is held in Australia and New Zealand?Vaibhav Sooryavanshi’s explosive 45 off 19 balls in the third T20I in Wellington has added to India’s selection headache. It’s a happy problem. Handed an opportunity after Ishan Kishan’s injury, Sooryavanshi initially struggled at No. 3 in Christchurch as he batted outside the Powerplay. But when India pushed him up to open alongside Abhishek Sharma in Wellington, the 15-year-old was back at his belligerent best. He smashed the first ball to the boundary and never looked back.While Abhishek’s century was the headline act, Sooryavanshi’s fearless approach set the tone. The pair raced to a stunning 133-run stand in just seven overs, blowing New Zealand away. The Abhishek-Sooryavanshi partnership also offered a glimpse into the mindset of a new generation of T20 batters, one that sees every ball as a scoring opportunity.The innings also carried a significant subplot. To accommodate Sooryavanshi at the top, Sanju Samson willingly moved down to No. 3 despite enjoying tremendous success as opener. Since returning to the side midway through the T20 World Cup, Samson has formed one of India’s most productive opening partnerships alongside Abhishek. Together, they have scored 1,166 runs in 37 matches and become permanent fixtures at the top of the order.Abhishek was quick to acknowledge the sacrifice. “The way Sanju bhai batted in the last game, it is not easy to let go of one’s familiar batting position. That showed his character.Someone’s going for his position but everyone is selfless and happy for each other, which is the hallmark of a great team,” he said in a BCCI video.The comment revealed an increasingly important characteristic of this Indian side. Unlike previous eras where players were tied to specific positions, this Indian team, under coach Gautam Gambhir , appears willing to embrace flexibility if it benefits the larger cause.That larger cause may now involve finding out just how good a Vaibhav-Abhishek opening pair can become. The youngster himself admitted that batting at No. 3 in Christchurch had forced him away from his natural game. “Last match, I went against my grain as to how I play in T20s. This game, I wanted to give a quick start so that it becomes easy,” Sooryavanshi said.His Wellington knock backed up that assessment. As an opener, there was visible clarity in his approach. He did not have to assess conditions or pace an innings. It was just all out attack.Abhishek, too, felt the impact from the other end. “When Vaibhav hit the first ball, he showed aggression. I saw that at the nonstriker’s end and when you see such a shot, you also feel pumped up. Special mention and credit to Vaibhav for how he played,” Abhishek said.The challenge now is fitting everyone into the same side when India are back at full strength. Sooryavanshi’s emergence during IPL 2026 makes it increasingly difficult to keep him on the bench. Yet India already have established performers in Samson and Kishan.However, the debate need not be framed as Vaibhav versus Sanju or Vaibhav versus Kishan. Head coach Gautam Gambhir has repeatedly maintained that only the top two batting positions are fixed and the rest of the order remains flexible. Kishan’s adaptability strengthens that approach.His matchwinning 80 off 46 balls at No. 5 during the Asian Games semifinal vs Sri Lanka showed he can thrive even when he is kept away from the opening slot. It also provided a possible blueprint on how all four batters can feature in the playing XI.With the series result already decided, India can afford to think beyond just the next game.
Article Summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's explosive 45 off 19 balls in the third T20I in Wellington has added to India’s selection headache. The 15-year-old smashed the first ball to the boundary and never looked back. The pair raced to a stunning 133-run stand in just seven overs.

Article Title: ‘Threatened and discriminated’: Kumar Sangakkara alleges discrimination by Ryanair staff in Dublin

Former Sri Lanka captain Kumar Sangakkara has alleged that Ryanair staff threatened and discriminated against his family at an airport in Dublin, with his account triggering a discussion on social media.The Rajasthan Royals head coach took to X on Wednesday evening to share his experience, describing the encounter with the airline's gate personnel as shocking. He also called it his first unpleasant experience in Dublin, the capital of Ireland.“Has anyone experienced discriminatory gate personnel @Ryanair in Dublin? I, with my family, just did and it was shocking," Sangakkara tweeted on Wednesday evening.Sangakkara's post drew reactions from social media users, including fellow Sri Lankan Sanjiva Weerawarana, who spoke about his own experiences of discrimination while living and travelling overseas.“Kumar, I have experienced discrimination in every part of the West. I lived there for 16 years, travelled back and forth for another 25 and now I’m done," the individual replied.Responding to Weerawarana, Sangakkara acknowledged the distress such encounters can cause.“It’s quite jarring when you experience it," Sangakkara said.The exchange added to the discussion surrounding the former Sri Lankan skipper's allegations and the treatment of passengers by airline personnel.At the time of writing, Ryanair had not issued a response to Sangakkara's claims.Ryanair is an Irish ultra-low-cost airline headquartered in Swords, County Dublin. The incident has also brought attention to concerns about anti-Asian racism and xenophobia in Ireland, which can range from everyday prejudice and online abuse to physical assaults.Sangakkara, regarded as one of Sri Lanka's greatest cricketers, retired from international cricket in 2015 after a distinguished career across formats.As Rajasthan Royals coach, Sangakkara ended the franchise’s 17-year wait to reach another final during his first tenure. His highest score was 169, while his tally included 25 centuries and 93 half-centuries.He brought his 50-over international career to an end after the 2015 World Cup in Australia and New Zealand. Sangakkara was part of Sri Lanka teams that finished runners-up at the 2007 and 2011 editions of the tournament.

Article Title: ‘Vaibhav heads out’: Ashwin’s blunt call on Sooryavanshi if Ishan Kishan returns

Former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin has called for patience with teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, urging fans and experts not to burden the youngster with expectations too early in his career. Ashwin also believes Sooryavanshi should make way for Sanju Samson at the top of the order if Ishan Kishan returns to the playing XI for the next T20I against New Zealand.Sooryavanshi made an immediate impact in the third T20I, hammering 45 off just 19 deliveries as India chased down a target of 199 with 6.4 overs to spare. The teenager shared a record-breaking 133-run opening stand with Abhishek Sharma, underlining his ability to take on the opposition from the outset.Praising the youngster's fearless approach, Ashwin said Sooryavanshi had already shown glimpses of his exceptional talent throughout the IPL and predicted a bright future for him."The way Vaibhav Sooryavanshi just took off was something that he has done all IPL. For me, he is and will always be a very special player. I look forward to seeing him do very many special things in his career," Ashwin said on SonyLiv.However, Ashwin feels Samson should reclaim his opening position if Kishan is available for the next match. With Kishan's injury having opened the door for Sooryavanshi, Samson had moved to No. 3 in the previous game.The veteran spinner believes Samson's experience makes him capable of adapting to the role, but his performances have earned him the right to open."In this combination, when Ishan Kishan is missing and Sooryavanshi has to come, that probably looks like the perfect order because Sanju has got the experience to be able to deal with going in at No. 3. However, tomorrow if Ishan Kishan is going to come back, I think Vaibhav heads out and Sanju slots right back into the slot he deserves," he added.Beyond the selection debate, Ashwin's bigger concern is ensuring that the 15-year-old gets enough room to develop without the weight of expectations. While acknowledging that Sooryavanshi could become one of Indian cricket's biggest names in the future, he stressed that the youngster should be allowed to enjoy the game."These are all big statements to make so early in his life. I really hope that the young boy gets that breathing space. I know he is going to be the poster boy of Indian cricket at some stage, but we all need to take that backward step and allow him to enjoy his cricket," said Ashwin.Drawing from his own early years in the game, Ashwin explained why it was important not to rush to conclusions about a young player's future based on a few standout performances."I have played cricket from a very young age, and at 16, I was enjoying cricket in the maidans in some club grounds in Chennai. That's what a 16-year-old is supposed to do. He did something spectacular today (Tuesday). I won't jump to any conclusions. He is a talent to watch out for. Let him enjoy his cricket, and let's also enjoy watching him bat," he explained.Sooryavanshi was drafted into the playing XI for the second T20I after Kishan picked up an injury, but struggled to make an impact at No. 3, scoring just four runs off eight balls.For the third T20I, Samson made way for the teenager at the top of the order, allowing him to partner Abhishek. The move paid off as the duo produced a record-breaking opening partnership to put India firmly on course for the chase.With Kishan potentially returning for the next game, the team management could face a decision over the batting order, with Ashwin backing Samson to resume his place as opener and Sooryavanshi to continue his development away from the immediate spotlight.
Article Summary: Former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin urges patience with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi. Ashwin believes the 15-year-old should make way for Sanju Samson at the top of the order if Ishan Kishan returns to the playing XI for the next T20I against New Zealand. The veteran spinner believes Samson's experience makes him capable of adapting to the role.
